title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

reading.body:
This is an impersonation carried out with a synthetic likeness, not a model that failed at a task it was given. Someone on a live WhatsApp video call presented themselves as a sitting chief minister, and the fabricated face and voice were the entry point for a scripted fraud. The script then added further invented authority, a supposed manager and a person claiming to be a CBI officer, so that each new payment demand arrived with a fresh official behind it. The generative tool did not malfunction here. It was the front door.

The failure sits at the point where a citizen has to decide, in real time, whether the person on the screen is who they appear to be. Nothing in that channel let the recipient verify the claim, and the only check in the loop was his own judgement, which held until the demands grew. Catching it would have required confirmation of the caller's identity through a channel independent of the call itself, or a check on whether any genuine aid scheme asks a recipient to pay processing fees before receiving money. Neither existed at the moment of contact.

What is not established is who was behind the call, and the registration of a case under the Information Technology Act is not a finding against anyone. The account rests on a single outlet's reporting, and the intent of the people involved has not been adjudicated.

reports.title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

summary:
A 29-year-old security guard in Bengaluru, Ratikanta Giri, from Odisha, received a WhatsApp video call on Sept 9 from someone using an AI deepfake to look and sound like Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay. The caller offered Rs 11 lakh in financial aid. A supposed manager then said Rs 5 lakh was allotted and asked for processing and other payments. Giri paid over Rs 1.04 lakh through a digital payment app after demands including Rs 5,000, Rs 18,000, and more than Rs 50,000 from a person claiming to be a CBI officer. This was the city's first reported case of its kind.

When the fraudsters asked for another Rs 50,000, Giri refused and realized he had been cheated. He contacted the cybercrime helpline 1930 and then approached Byappanahalli police. A case has been registered under the Information Technology Act. Police advised people not to believe such calls or make payments based on such claims.
